name: Seismic Resonance Charge SRC-2
description:
The SRC-2 does not detonate in the conventional sense. It anchors to a surface via four magnetized contact prongs and then drives a precisely tuned low-frequency resonance pulse directly into the substrate — concrete, steel plate, composite flooring, even packed earth. The pulse is calibrated to match the structural resonance frequency of the target material, which the charge's onboard sensor array calculates in the 0.8 seconds after contact. At resonance frequency, the charge amplifies the vibration in a compounding wave pattern until the structural integrity of the material fails catastrophically from within. The external surface may show no visible damage until the moment of collapse.

The SRC-2's defining characteristic is that its destructive energy is entirely directional — downward and outward through the substrate, not upward into open air. Personnel standing on the affected surface experience the failure as the floor or wall simply ceasing to exist beneath them. There is no pressure wave, no heat, no shrapnel — just sudden, catastrophic structural dissolution. This makes standard blast-protection gear completely irrelevant. Hardened armor rated for conventional explosives offers no protection whatsoever if the floor you are standing on liquefies into rubble.

Palladian Construction originally developed resonance-charge technology for controlled demolition of legacy infrastructure in GLMZ's lower wards — a way to drop a building precisely without disturbing adjacent structures. The SRC-2 is a direct weaponization of that demolition patent, adapted by a third-party contractor that Palladian has spent four years unsuccessfully suing into nonexistence. The original demolition variant required a licensed operator and a 48-hour structural survey. The SRC-2 requires neither.
specifications:
weight: 2.3 kg
anchor mechanism: Four-point magnetic contact prongs, rated for steel, concrete, and composite
frequency scan time: 0.8 seconds post-contact
effective radius: 3–7 meters substrate disruption (material-dependent)
energy source: Solid-state capacitor bank, single-use
blast profile: No conventional overpressure; structural failure propagates through substrate
arming delay: User-configurable, 2–30 seconds
countermeasure vulnerability: Frequency-jamming fields can interrupt scan cycle if deployed within 0.8-second window
tactical_use: The SRC-2 is used almost exclusively for structural breaching and denial operations. Operators plant it on load-bearing floors, walls, or support columns and withdraw before detonation. In multi-story facilities, a single charge placed on a central column can collapse an entire floor section, cutting off pursuit or eliminating a fortified position from below. It is also used offensively in scenarios where targets are wearing blast-hardened gear — the charge's non-conventional damage profile bypasses armor entirely. Some operators use it to breach vaults or reinforced rooms by destroying the structural integrity of the surrounding material rather than attacking the hardened door directly.
cultural_context: In GLMZ, the SRC-2 has become a symbol of a particular kind of street-level ingenuity — taking corporate infrastructure technology and turning it against corporate infrastructure. Demolition crews in the lower wards sometimes encounter the weapon's aftermath and recognize the resonance pattern from their own legitimate tools, which creates a strange professional kinship with whoever deployed it. Certain radical urban reclamation groups have adopted the SRC-2 as an ideological weapon, using it to collapse corporate-owned development sites. Among conventional arms dealers, it has a reputation for being almost impossible to trace back to a buyer because the structural failure it causes reads as ordinary building collapse.
known_users: Structural saboteur archetype known as 'the Architect'
Corporate counter-espionage teams targeting rival facility infrastructure
story_hooks: A series of 'accidental' building collapses in a contested development zone are actually SRC-2 deployments — but the charges are being planted by someone inside Palladian Construction itself, using access to the original demolition patent to cover their tracks.

A player character is inside a building when the floor begins to fail in a pattern that a demolitions-savvy ally recognizes as resonance collapse. They have approximately 90 seconds before the structural failure reaches their level.
Ringo's shell subsidiary is being investigated, but the investigator keeps dying in building collapses that look accidental. The pattern is too consistent to be coincidence.

A Palladian engineer approaches the players with evidence that someone inside the company has been licensing the SRC-2 technology illegally — and that the buyer list includes several names that should not have access to demolition-grade ordnance.

physical_description.visual_profile: A compact, angular device resembling a metallic starfish or angular clamp. The form is deliberately geometric — four splayed magnetic prongs radiate from a central cylindrical core, creating a low, aggressive silhouette designed for rapid deployment and secure contact.
physical_description.dimensions: Central body: 12cm diameter, 8cm height. Magnetic prongs extend 6cm outward when deployed. Total footprint when anchored: approximately 24cm across.
physical_description.weight_description: Dense and purposeful — 2.3kg feels substantial in hand but not unwieldy. The weight is concentrated in the core, making it easy to place with precision despite the prong assembly.
physical_description.primary_material: Reinforced titanium-composite alloy frame with hardened steel magnetic contact prongs. Internal capacitor bank housed in a sealed pressure chamber.
physical_description.finish: Matte gunmetal gray with industrial texture to reduce reflectivity. The prongs are brushed steel with faint corrosion patterns suggesting field use.
physical_description.color_scheme: Gunmetal gray primary body with darker charcoal accents around the prong assembly. Minimal color — function over aesthetics.
physical_description.grip_texture: The central body features a deeply textured, rubberized grip section with subtle ridges for positive hold even with gloved hands. Designed for one-handed placement.
distinctive_features: Four splayed magnetic contact prongs with visible contact surfaces
Central cylindrical body with recessed arming dial (2–30 second adjustment knob)
Small LED status indicator array (red/amber/green) mounted on the top surface
Micro-sensor vents along the base — barely visible grilles housing the resonance-detection array
Faint Halloran Security Consulting logo etched into one prong
Thermally discolored patches on the prongs from previous deployments
Subtle manufacturing serial number stamped on the underside of the body
physical_description.manufacturer_markings: Halloran Security Consulting logo (a stylized shield within crosshairs) etched subtly into the upper surface of one magnetic prong. Serial number stamped in small font on the underside. No product name visible — designed for anonymity.
physical_description.condition_typical: Well-maintained but battle-worn. The prongs show micro-scratches from repeated contact with concrete and steel. The rubberized grip section is darkened from handling oils and dirt. No major damage, but the device reads as a tool that has seen field deployment — scuffed, functional, and deliberately inconspicuous.
